lessons.title: 1. Translate a rule into logic
lessons.takeaway: Check each condition separately before combining conditions.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A proposition has a truth value. For a download rule, let A mean that the account is active and B mean that the file is public. A and B permits a download only when both statements are true. A or B permits either statement or both. Write the four possible input pairs to check the rule before using it in code.

Negation changes true to false and false to true. The rule not (A and B) is equivalent to (not A) or (not B). It is not equivalent to (not A) and (not B). With Boolean inputs these expressions form a truth table; with other Python objects, `and` and `or` can return an operand rather than a `bool`.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: An active account requesting a private file has A=True and B=False. The conjunction rejects it. Negating that conjunction accepts this pair because at least one required condition failed.

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: A logical implication does not say its converse is true. If passing the check requires an active account, an active account can still fail another check.

exercise.prompt: A request is accepted when the user is active and either owns the file or the file is public. Write the condition and test an inactive owner and an active non-owner of a public file.
exercise.solution:
accepted = active and (owns_file or public)
# inactive owner: False
# active non-owner, public file: True
checks: Parentheses group the two access reasons.
An inactive user is rejected even when they own the file.

quiz.question: Which expression equals not (A or B) for Boolean values?
quiz.explanation: Both statements must be false for their OR to be false. Negating each separately and joining with AND expresses that case.

lessons.title: 2. Count unique items and overlap
lessons.takeaway: Subtract overlap once when combining two sets.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A set records membership without duplicates or order. Intersection contains members shared by both sets. Union contains members present in either set. Difference A - B contains members in A that are absent from B, so reversing the operands changes the question.

Adding the two set sizes counts every shared member twice. The union size is len(A) + len(B) - len(A & B). This reasoning also explains why a join can inflate a count when you intended to count unique people.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Three people read Python and two read SQL. Bea appears in both groups, so there are four people in the union, not five.

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: Turning purchases into a set of customer IDs deliberately discards repeat purchases. Keep a list when multiplicity is part of the question.

exercise.prompt: A={1,2,3,4} and B={3,4,5}. Find the intersection, union and members only in B.
checks: Union has five unique members.
Only-in-B uses B - A.

quiz.question: A has 10 members, B has 8 and their intersection has 3. How many are in their union?
quiz.explanation: The three shared members were included twice in 10 + 8. Subtract them once to obtain 15.

lessons.title: 3. Read a function and its domain
lessons.takeaway: A formula needs a stated set of valid inputs.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A mathematical function assigns one output to each input in its domain. The rule cost(q)=50+12q maps an order quantity to its cost in cents. Its domain might be nonnegative integers because an order cannot contain a fractional item. The formula alone does not enforce that business rule.

Composition feeds one function into another. If bytes(size_mb)=size_mb*1_000_000 and seconds(bytes)=bytes/250_000, then seconds(bytes(2)) is 8. Track what each intermediate value means; reversing the functions would mix incompatible inputs.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: For q=3 the fixed fee contributes 50 cents and the items contribute 36 cents. The result is 86 cents. For zero items the formula still gives 50, so decide whether an empty order is actually allowed.

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: A Python function can read time or mutate a list. The mathematical model here assumes a fixed rule, so identical inputs give identical outputs.

exercise.prompt: Define f(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=x*x. Calculate g(f(3)) and f(g(3)). Explain why they differ.
exercise.solution:
g(f(3)) = g(7) = 49.
f(g(3)) = f(9) = 19.
The order of applying the rules changes the result.
checks: Compute the inner function first.
Do not assume composition commutes.

quiz.question: The rule time=distance/speed accepts speed=0. What is missing?
options: A domain restriction that excludes zero speed
quiz.explanation: Division by zero is undefined. A travel-time model normally requires a positive speed and compatible distance units.

lessons.title: 4. Keep units in a calculation
lessons.takeaway: Rates combine quantities with different units.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Write the unit beside each number before calculating. Dividing 1,200 requests by 60 seconds gives 20 requests per second. Multiplying that rate by 15 seconds gives 300 requests. Seconds cancel; the remaining unit describes the answer.

An average rate over several periods uses total work divided by total time. Equal-duration periods let you average their rates without weights. Otherwise, weight each rate by its duration; an unweighted average can give the wrong result. Decimal MB means 1,000,000 bytes here; binary MiB means 1,048,576 bytes. State which unit a size uses.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: A service completes 100 requests in 10 seconds and 100 more in 30 seconds. Across the whole observation it completes 200 in 40 seconds, or 5 per second. Averaging 10 and 3.333 would give the wrong total rate.
sections.example:
counts = [100, 100]
seconds = [10, 30]
print(sum(counts) / sum(seconds))  # 5.0

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: A measured throughput is not a guarantee for a larger workload. Queueing, caching and resource limits can change the rate.

exercise.prompt: A 6 MB file transfers at 500,000 bytes per second. Ignoring overhead, calculate seconds. Then calculate the average rate for 6 MB in 12 seconds and 4 MB in 20 seconds.
checks: Convert MB to bytes before dividing.
Aggregate bytes and seconds before computing the second rate.

quiz.question: Two equal-sized files take 2 and 6 seconds. Which denominator gives their combined throughput?
options: The average of the two speeds
quiz.explanation: Total throughput divides the combined file size by all eight elapsed seconds.

lessons.title: 5. Choose the percentage denominator
lessons.takeaway: A percentage change uses the original value as its denominator.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: The fraction part/whole becomes a percentage after multiplication by 100. A change from old to new uses (new-old)/old. The denominator answers the question "relative to what?" A zero old value makes this relative change undefined, even when the absolute change is clear.

A rate moving from 20% to 25% rises by five percentage points. Its relative increase is 5/20=25%. Consecutive percentage changes multiply. A 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease does not return to the starting value because the second change uses a different base.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Starting with 100 units, an increase of 20% produces 120. Reducing the new amount by 20% removes 24 units and leaves 96.
sections.example:
start = 100
end = start * 1.20 * 0.80
print(end)  # 96.0

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: Do not average subgroup percentages without their denominators. One success out of two and nine out of ten combine to 10/12, not the average of 50% and 90%.

exercise.prompt: Errors fall from 50 to 40. Report the absolute change and relative change. A success rate rises from 0.80 to 0.90; report percentage-point and relative changes.
exercise.solution:
Errors change by -10, or -10/50 = -20%.
Success rises by 10 percentage points, or 0.10/0.80 = 12.5%.
checks: The original count is the denominator.
Distinguish percentage points from percent change.

quiz.question: A value doubles and then halves. Where does it end?
quiz.explanation: Multiplying by 2 and then by 0.5 gives an overall multiplier of 1.

lessons.title: 6. Compare additive and multiplicative growth
lessons.takeaway: Repeated proportional changes multiply rather than add.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Adding the same amount each step gives linear growth. Multiplying by the same factor gives exponential growth. After k doublings, a starting quantity x becomes x*2**k. The exponent counts multiplications, not an amount added to the original value.

A logarithm reverses exponentiation. If 2**k=32, then k=5. In computing, repeatedly halving a problem of size 32 takes five halvings to reach one. State the base when interpreting a numerical logarithm, and distinguish exact powers from cases requiring a rounded number of whole steps.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Starting with eight records, three doublings produce 64 records. Adding eight three times instead produces 32. These models agree at the first step but diverge afterward.

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: A measured trend over a short period does not justify indefinite exponential growth. A real system can hit storage, demand or capacity limits.

exercise.prompt: A collection starts with 5 records and triples each round. How many records exist after four rounds? How many halvings take 64 items down to one?
exercise.solution:
5 * 3**4 = 405 records.
64,32,16,8,4,2,1 takes six halvings.
checks: The initial state is round zero.
Count transitions, not the seven listed states.

quiz.question: A loop halves an exact power-of-two size until it reaches one. Doubling the starting size adds how many iterations?
quiz.explanation: One extra halving removes the additional factor of two.

lessons.title: 7. Undo growth with logarithms and read log scales
lessons.takeaway: A logarithm counts how many times you multiply by the base; equal steps on a log scale are equal ratios.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: `log2(1024) = 10` because 2 multiplied by itself 10 times is 1024. A logarithm undoes a power: if `b**x = y`, then `log_b(y) = x`. Base 10 counts digits (a six-figure number has a base-10 log between 5 and 6), base 2 counts halvings or doublings, and the natural log uses e, which appears in continuous growth.

Logarithms turn multiplication into addition: `log(a*b) = log(a) + log(b)`. That is why they answer "how many periods?" questions about compound growth from lesson 6. Growing by a factor r per period reaches k times the start after `log(k) / log(r)` periods; at 7% per period, doubling takes about 10.24 periods.

A log scale on a chart spaces 10, 100 and 1000 equally, because each is ten times the last. Use it when values span several orders of magnitude, or when relative change matters more than absolute change, such as latency percentiles or growth curves. A straight line on a log-scaled y-axis means steady percentage growth.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Binary search halves a sorted list each step, so a million items need at most `ceil(log2(1,000,000)) = 20` comparisons. On a log scale, 10 → 100 → 1000 → 10000 are steps of exactly 1.
sections.example:
import math

print(math.log2(1024), math.log10(1_000_000))
print(round(math.log(2) / math.log(1.07), 2), 'periods to double at 7% growth')
print(math.ceil(math.log2(1_000_000)), 'halvings to search a million sorted items')
values = [10, 100, 1000, 10000]
print([round(math.log10(b) - math.log10(a), 6) for a, b in zip(values, values[1:])])

# Expected output:
# 10.0 6.0
# 10.24 periods to double at 7% growth
# 20 halvings to search a million sorted items
# [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: Logarithms are defined only for positive numbers. Zero or negative values (refunds, zero-latency samples) need handling before a log transform or a log axis, and adding a constant such as `log(x + 1)` changes the meaning near zero.
A log axis makes large differences look small. Label it clearly, and do not compare the visual gap between two lines as if the axis were linear.

exercise.prompt: A user base grows 5% each month from 2,000 users. Use logarithms to find how many whole months until it first exceeds 10,000, then check by repeated multiplication.
exercise.solution:
Months = log(10000/2000) / log(1.05) = log(5) / log(1.05) ≈ 32.99, so the first whole month above 10,000 is month 33.
Check: 2000 × 1.05**32 ≈ 9,529 (below), 2000 × 1.05**33 ≈ 10,005 (above).
checks: Divides log of the ratio by log of the growth factor.
Rounds up to the first whole month that exceeds the target.
Confirms with the neighbouring months.

quiz.question: On a chart with a log-scaled y-axis, a metric moves from 100 to 1,000 and later from 1,000 to 10,000. How do the two moves look?
options: The second looks ten times taller
They look the same height, because each is a tenfold increase
quiz.explanation: A log scale maps equal ratios to equal distances, so two tenfold increases cover the same vertical span.

lessons.title: 8. Solve for an unknown and check it
lessons.takeaway: Reverse the operations, then substitute the answer into the original equation.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Algebra preserves equality by applying the same operation to both sides. For 5+3x=20, subtract 5 from both sides and divide both sides by 3. The result x=5 is only a candidate until you substitute it back and check that both sides equal 20.

A model can be mathematically solvable but inappropriate for the input. If x counts machines it must be a nonnegative integer. A capacity requirement such as 3x>=16 needs x>=16/3, so six whole machines are required. Rounding to five would violate the inequality.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: A fictional batch has a fixed two-second setup and costs three seconds per item. To fit a 20-second limit, 2+3n<=20 gives n<=6. Six items fit exactly; seven take 23 seconds.
sections.example:
limit, setup, per_item = 20, 2, 3
n = (limit - setup) // per_item
print(n, setup + per_item * n)  # 6 20

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: Floating-point arithmetic can make equality checks fragile. For measured decimal values use an appropriate tolerance; do not use rounding to hide a model that fails its unit or domain checks.

exercise.prompt: A fee is 8+4q cents. Find q when the total is 36. Under a 35-cent limit, what is the largest whole q?
exercise.solution:
4q = 28, so q = 7; substituting gives 36.
Under 35 cents, q <= 27/4 = 6.75. The largest whole q is 6, which costs 32 cents.
checks: Substitute q=7 into the equality.
Check both 6 and 7 against the limit.

quiz.question: A capacity rule needs n>=4.2 whole workers. Which count satisfies it?
quiz.explanation: Four is below the lower bound. Rounding upward to five respects the inequality.

lessons.title: 9. Compare centre and distribution
lessons.takeaway: A single average can hide an uneven distribution.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: The arithmetic mean shares the total equally among observations. The median is the middle ordered observation, or the mean of the two middle observations for an even-sized list. Sorting changes positions without changing the total, so the mean does not require sorting.

Inspect the observations before choosing a summary. A high value can move the mean strongly while leaving the median unchanged. That is not a reason to delete it: a genuine long delay may matter more than the typical delay. Report units and the number of observations.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Latencies of 10, 10, 10, 10 and 100 milliseconds have mean 28 and median 10. The mean reflects the slow request; the median describes the middle request. Both calculations are correct.
sections.example:
from statistics import mean, median
x = [10, 10, 10, 10, 100]
print(mean(x), median(x))  # 28 10

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: Missing observations are not zeros. A missing duration and an actual zero duration have different meanings and can change both summaries.

exercise.prompt: For [2,3,3,4,18], calculate mean and median. Replace 18 with 180 and recalculate both. Explain which summary changed most.
exercise.solution:
Original mean=30/5=6, median=3.
New mean=192/5=38.4, median=3.
Only the mean changes because the middle ordered observation stays 3.
checks: Retain all five observations.
Explain the unchanged median using ordered positions.

quiz.question: A dashboard shows only median latency. What can it conceal?
options: A small group of extremely slow requests
quiz.explanation: A small slow group may barely move the middle observation. Inspect spread and upper-tail values as well.

lessons.title: 10. Measure spread around the mean
lessons.takeaway: Variance averages squared deviations; standard deviation restores the original unit.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Subtract the mean from each value to get deviations. Their signed sum is zero, so averaging those deviations cannot measure spread. Squaring removes the signs. Population variance divides the sum of squared deviations by N when describing the full set of interest.

For an independent sample used to estimate population variance, the usual sample variance divides by n-1. Estimating the mean from the same sample uses one degree of freedom. Standard deviation is the square root of variance. It has the data unit; variance has that unit squared.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: For [2,4,6], the mean is 4 and squared deviations are 4,0,4. Population variance is 8/3; sample variance is 8/2=4. The sample standard deviation is 2.
sections.example:
from statistics import pvariance, variance, stdev
x = [2, 4, 6]
print(pvariance(x), variance(x), stdev(x))
# 2.6666666666666665 4 2.0

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: A larger standard deviation does not identify the cause of variation. Time order, distinct subgroups or a bad measurement can produce the same numerical spread.

exercise.prompt: Find population variance and sample variance for [1,1,5,5]. State the standard deviation unit if these values are seconds.
exercise.solution:
Mean=3. Squared deviations total 16.
Population variance=16/4=4; sample variance=16/3.
Standard deviation is in seconds; variance is in seconds squared.
checks: Use four in the population denominator.
Use three in the sample denominator.

quiz.question: Why does the reference reject sample variance for one observation?
quiz.explanation: A sample of one leaves no degrees of freedom for this variance estimate. Its mean is still defined.

lessons.title: 11. Build a finite probability model
lessons.takeaway: Count outcomes only after stating which outcomes are equally likely.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A sample space lists possible outcomes. An event is a subset of those outcomes. For a uniformly chosen item in a finite list, its event probability is the number of matching outcomes divided by the number of possible outcomes. If outcomes have unequal chances, counting alone is insufficient.

An event and its complement divide the sample space without overlap. Their probabilities add to one. The probability of at least one failure is often easier to obtain by subtracting the probability of no failures from one. Multiplying probabilities requires an independence assumption or conditional probabilities.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Two independent fair coin tosses have four equally likely ordered outcomes. Only TT contains no heads, so at least one head has probability 1-1/4=3/4.
sections.example:
from itertools import product
outcomes = list(product("HT", repeat=2))
print(sum("H" in x for x in outcomes) / len(outcomes))  # 0.75

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: Two requests reaching the same failing server may have dependent outcomes. Treating their failure events as independent can badly underestimate joint failure.

exercise.prompt: Three independent attempts each fail with probability 0.2. Find the chance that all fail and the chance at least one succeeds.
exercise.solution:
All fail: 0.2**3 = 0.008.
At least one succeeds: 1 - 0.008 = 0.992.
checks: State independence.
Use the complement of all failing, not of one failing.

quiz.question: A die is loaded. Is counting three even faces out of six enough to prove P(even)=0.5?
options: Yes, even and odd are complements
quiz.explanation: Complementary events sum to one but need not have equal probabilities. Equal face counts work only with a uniform die.

lessons.title: 12. Change the denominator when conditioning
lessons.takeaway: A conditional probability counts within the group named after "given".

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: P(A given B) asks how often A occurs among cases where B occurs. With counts it is count(A and B)/count(B), provided count(B)>0. The denominator shrinks to B. Reversing A and B usually changes that denominator and the answer.

Independence means learning B does not change the probability of A. Disjoint events cannot both occur; independent events can. For two disjoint events with positive probabilities, observing one makes the other impossible, so they are dependent.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Among 100 files, 10 are corrupted. A checker flags eight corrupted files and nine clean files. Among the 17 flagged files, eight are corrupted: 8/17, about 47.1%. The checker finding 8/10 corrupted files answers a different question.
sections.example:
flagged_corrupt, flagged_clean = 8, 9
print(flagged_corrupt / (flagged_corrupt + flagged_clean))
# 0.47058823529411764

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: The proportion of corrupted files in the population affects the meaning of a positive result. A measured detection rate alone cannot give the probability that a flagged file is corrupted.

exercise.prompt: Of 200 events, 20 are failures. An alert catches 15 failures and also flags 30 successes. Compute P(alert given failure) and P(failure given alert).
exercise.solution:
P(alert | failure)=15/20=0.75.
P(failure | alert)=15/45=1/3.
The denominators are failures and alerts respectively.
checks: Count all 45 alerts in the second denominator.
Do not interpret 75% detection as 75% alert precision.
hints: Write the two denominators before dividing: all failures, then all alerts.
Alerts include failures and successes.
pitfalls: Using the 20 failures as the denominator for both questions.
Reading a detection rate as the share of alerts that are real.

options: No, this formula divides by zero
quiz.explanation: The elementary conditional-probability formula requires P(B)>0. The reference rejects an empty conditioned group.

practice.prompt: In the lesson's 100 files, 10 are corrupted, and the checker flags 8 corrupted and 9 clean files. Supply the two missing conditional probabilities: P(flagged | clean) and P(clean | not flagged).
hints: Fill in all four cells of the flagged/not-flagged by corrupted/clean table first.
practice.solution: Clean files: 90, of which 9 are flagged, so P(flagged | clean) = 9 / 90 = 0.1. Files not flagged: 100 − 17 = 83, of which 90 − 9 = 81 are clean, so P(clean | not flagged) = 81 / 83 ≈ 0.976. Each question has its own denominator: clean files, then unflagged files.
checks: Uses clean files as the first denominator.
Uses unflagged files as the second.
Computes both values.

practice.prompt: Same checker, which flags 80% of corrupted files and 10% of clean ones, but now 10 of 1,000 files are corrupted. What is P(corrupted | flagged)?
hints: Count flagged corrupted and flagged clean files separately.
practice.solution: Flagged corrupted files: 10 × 0.8 = 8. Flagged clean files: 990 × 0.1 = 99. P(corrupted | flagged) = 8 / (8 + 99) = 8 / 107 ≈ 0.075, down from about 0.471 in the lesson. The checker did not change; the rarer corruption made most flags false.
checks: Applies each rate to its own group.
Computes the new conditional probability.
Explains the change through the base rate.

practice.prompt: P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5. Are A and B independent if P(A and B) = 0.15? If P(A and B) = 0.2? And if A and B are disjoint?
hints: Compute P(A | B) in each case and compare it with P(A).
practice.solution: Independence means P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.15. With 0.15 they are independent: P(A | B) = 0.15 / 0.5 = 0.3 = P(A). With 0.2, P(A | B) = 0.4, so learning B changes A: dependent. If they are disjoint, P(A and B) = 0, so P(A | B) = 0 ≠ 0.3: disjoint events with positive probabilities are always dependent.
checks: Uses the product rule as the test.
Decides each of the three cases.

practice.prompt: A vendor says its fraud detector 'catches 99% of fraud'. Is that enough to decide whether its alerts are worth investigating?
hints: Which conditional probability does the 99% describe?
practice.solution: No. 99% is P(alert | fraud). To know what share of alerts are fraud you also need the false alert rate on legitimate payments and the fraud base rate in your traffic. Ask for both, or run the detector on a labelled sample of your own payments.

lessons.title: 13. Update a probability with Bayes' theorem
lessons.takeaway: P(cause | evidence) depends on how common the cause was to begin with, not only on how accurate the evidence is.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Lesson 12 showed that conditioning changes the denominator. Bayes' theorem turns a conditional probability around: `P(A | B) = P(B | A) × P(A) / P(B)`. A test's accuracy gives `P(positive | condition)`; the question people care about is `P(condition | positive)`.

`P(B)` usually needs the law of total probability: positives come from true cases and from false alarms, `P(positive) = P(positive | condition) × P(condition) + P(positive | no condition) × P(no condition)`. The starting probability `P(condition)` is the base rate or prior; the result is the posterior.

When the base rate is low, even an accurate test produces mostly false alarms, because the many people without the condition generate more false positives than the few with it generate true positives. Counting a concrete population, such as 10,000 people, makes this visible and avoids arithmetic slips.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: A fraud rule flags 95% of fraudulent payments and 5% of legitimate ones, and 1% of payments are fraudulent. Of 10,000 payments, 95 fraudulent ones are flagged and 495 legitimate ones are flagged too. Only about 16% of flagged payments are fraud, although the rule is "95% accurate".
sections.example:
base_rate, sensitivity, false_positive_rate = 0.01, 0.95, 0.05

p_flag = sensitivity * base_rate + false_positive_rate * (1 - base_rate)
posterior = sensitivity * base_rate / p_flag
print(f'P(flagged) = {p_flag:.4f}, P(fraud | flagged) = {posterior:.3f}')

payments = 10_000
fraud = payments * base_rate
true_flags = round(fraud * sensitivity)
false_flags = round((payments - fraud) * false_positive_rate)
print(true_flags, 'true flags,', false_flags, 'false flags')

# Expected output:
# P(flagged) = 0.0590, P(fraud | flagged) = 0.161
# 95 true flags, 495 false flags

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: The base rate must describe the population being tested. A rule applied only to payments already flagged by another system sees a much higher fraud rate, and its posterior changes accordingly.

Sensitivity and false-positive rates are themselves estimates, often measured on a different population. Report the posterior with that uncertainty, and use Bayes' theorem to ask which input most changes the decision before collecting more data.

Applies sensitivity to outages and the false-positive rate to healthy checks.
Divides real alerts by all alerts.

Apply 90% to one group and 2% to the other.
pitfalls: Applying the false-positive rate to all checks instead of healthy ones.
Reporting 90% as the share of alerts that are real.

options: The many people without the condition produce more false positives than the few with it produce true positives
Bayes' theorem only applies to medicine
quiz.explanation: With a low base rate, a small false-positive rate applied to a large healthy group can outnumber the true positives.

practice.prompt: In the lesson's fraud rule (95% sensitivity, 5% false positive rate), the base rate rises to 10%. Supply P(flagged) and P(fraud | flagged).
hints: Positives come from fraud cases and from false alarms.
practice.solution: P(flagged) = 0.95 × 0.10 + 0.05 × 0.90 = 0.095 + 0.045 = 0.140. P(fraud | flagged) = 0.095 / 0.140 ≈ 0.679. With ten times more fraud, about two thirds of flags are real instead of about 16%.
checks: Uses total probability for P(flagged).
Divides the true-flag share by it.

practice.prompt: Back to a 1% base rate, but the false positive rate is halved to 2.5%. What fraction of flags are fraud now?
hints: Which term in the denominator is larger?
practice.solution: P(flagged) = 0.95 × 0.01 + 0.025 × 0.99 = 0.0095 + 0.02475 = 0.03425. P(fraud | flagged) = 0.0095 / 0.03425 ≈ 0.277. Halving false alarms raised precision from about 16% to about 28%; with rare fraud, the false positive rate matters more than sensitivity.
checks: Recomputes P(flagged).
Compares with the original posterior.

practice.prompt: A payment is flagged by the rule, giving P(fraud) ≈ 0.161. A second, independent rule with the same rates also flags it. Use 0.161 as the new prior: what is P(fraud) now?
hints: Replace the 1% base rate with 0.161.
practice.solution: P(fraud | both) = 0.95 × 0.161 / (0.95 × 0.161 + 0.05 × 0.839) ≈ 0.153 / 0.195 ≈ 0.785. Each independent flag is evidence that updates the previous posterior. If the rules share inputs, their flags are not independent and this overstates the evidence.
checks: Uses the first posterior as the prior.
Computes the updated probability.
Notes the independence assumption.

practice.prompt: The rule is moved to run only on payments that another system has already flagged, where 20% are fraud. Can you keep quoting '16% of flags are fraud'?
hints: Which input changed?
practice.solution: No. The base rate is now 20%: P(fraud | flagged) = 0.95 × 0.2 / (0.95 × 0.2 + 0.05 × 0.8) = 0.19 / 0.23 ≈ 0.826. Recompute the posterior for each population the rule is applied to, and check that the rates still hold there.
checks: Recomputes with the new base rate.

lessons.title: 14. Separate sampling noise from selection bias
lessons.takeaway: A large sample can still miss the population you mean to describe.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Define the population before choosing observations. If the question is about all users, a survey of only users who completed a course excludes people who left. Increasing the number of completers surveyed reduces some sampling noise but does not repair that exclusion.

A random sample uses a known selection process. Different random samples usually give different summaries. This sampling variation is distinct from a systematic measurement error or a missing group. Record the sampling unit too: 100 requests from one user are not 100 independently sampled users.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: A fictional population has durations [2,4,6,8]. The six equally likely samples of two without replacement have means 3,4,5,5,6,7. Their average is the population mean 5, although an individual sample need not equal 5.
sections.example:
from itertools import combinations
from statistics import mean
means = [mean(s) for s in combinations([2,4,6,8], 2)]
print(means, mean(means))  # [3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7] 5

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: A random seed makes a simulation repeatable; it does not make a biased sampling method representative. A fixed seed is useful for debugging, not evidence that one sample is typical.

exercise.prompt: A site asks only paying users about ease of signup. The team wants a claim about everyone who started signup. Name the missing group and one better collection method.
exercise.solution: People who abandoned signup or never paid are missing. Sample people who started signup, including non-completers, and track nonresponse. A larger paying-user sample alone cannot resolve the omission.
checks: Identify non-completers.
Keep nonresponse as a remaining limitation.

quiz.question: Which change addresses a selection problem?
options: Survey ten times as many members of the same excluded-group design
Include the previously excluded target group in the sampling frame
Round the mean to fewer decimals
quiz.explanation: Coverage changes who can enter the sample. More observations or fewer decimals do not restore a missing group.

lessons.title: 15. Weight outcomes by their probabilities
lessons.takeaway: Expected value is a probability-weighted average, not a guaranteed outcome.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: For a finite distribution, multiply each numerical outcome by its probability and add the products. Probabilities must be nonnegative and sum to one. The expected value describes a long-run average under repeated comparable trials; it need not equal any possible individual outcome.

Linearity of expectation lets you add expected contributions even when the contributions are dependent. Independence is a separate issue when calculating a joint probability or the variability of a sum. Expected value alone also omits the size of rare adverse outcomes.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: A job takes one second with probability 0.9 and eleven seconds with probability 0.1. Its expected duration is 0.9*1+0.1*11=2 seconds. No individual run takes exactly two seconds in this model.
sections.example:
durations = [1,11]
probabilities = [.9,.1]
print(sum(x*p for x,p in zip(durations,probabilities)))  # 2.0

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: A timeout set to the mean would fail on every eleven-second run. A service decision often needs the distribution tail as well as the mean.

exercise.prompt: An operation costs 2 units with probability 0.75 and 10 units with probability 0.25. Calculate its expected cost and the expected total cost for 20 such operations with the same marginal distribution.
exercise.solution:
Expected cost is .75*2+.25*10=4 units.
Expected total is 20*4=80 units. Independence is unnecessary for this expectation, although it affects variability.
checks: Do not average 2 and 10 without weights.
Do not claim every batch costs exactly 80.
hints: Multiply each cost by its probability, then add.
For 20 operations, linearity lets you add expected costs.
pitfalls: Claiming every batch of 20 costs exactly 80.

quiz.question: Expected cost is 4, but outcomes are 2 or 10. Is the calculation necessarily wrong?
options: Yes, an average must be an outcome
No, a weighted average can lie between outcomes
quiz.explanation: An expected value summarizes the distribution and need not be an attainable single result.

practice.prompt: The lesson's job takes 1 second with probability 0.9 and 11 seconds with probability 0.1, with mean 2. Supply the variance and standard deviation, using Var = E[X²] − (E[X])².
hints: Square each outcome before weighting.
practice.solution: E[X²] = 0.9 × 1 + 0.1 × 121 = 13. Var = 13 − 2² = 9, so the standard deviation is 3 seconds. A spread larger than the mean signals that the mean alone hides the slow runs.
checks: Computes E[X²].
Subtracts the squared mean.

practice.prompt: A request fails with probability 0.2, independently each time, and is retried until it succeeds. What is the expected number of attempts, and what share of requests need more than 3?
hints: The chance that the first k attempts all fail is 0.2 to the power k.
practice.solution: Attempts follow a geometric distribution with success probability 0.8, so the mean is 1 / 0.8 = 1.25 attempts. More than 3 attempts means the first 3 fail: 0.2³ = 0.008, or 0.8% of requests. The mean is small, but the tail decides how long to wait.
checks: Uses 1 / p for the mean.
Computes the tail probability.

practice.prompt: You can pay 5 units for insurance against a 1% chance of losing 400 units. What is the expected loss without insurance, and does expected value settle the decision?
hints: Compare the premium with probability times loss.
practice.solution: Expected loss = 0.01 × 400 = 4 units, less than the 5-unit premium, so on expected value alone you would not insure. Expected value ignores how much one loss of 400 would hurt. If that loss is unaffordable, paying 1 unit more than its expected cost can be the right choice.
checks: Computes the expected loss.
Explains what expected value leaves out.

practice.prompt: Someone proposes setting the job's timeout to its expected duration, 2 seconds. What happens?
hints: Which runs take longer than 2 seconds?
practice.solution: Every 11-second run times out: 10% of runs fail, although nothing is wrong with them. Set timeouts from the distribution's tail, such as a high percentile plus margin, not from the mean.
checks: Computes the share of runs that time out.
Recommends a percentile-based timeout.

lessons.title: 16. Recognise binomial and normal distributions
lessons.takeaway: Counts of independent yes/no trials follow a binomial distribution; many sums and averages are close to normal, where 68%, 95% and 99.7% fall within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A distribution assigns probabilities to every possible value. The binomial distribution counts successes in n independent trials that each succeed with probability p, such as failed requests out of 20 when each fails 10% of the time: `P(k) = C(n, k) × p**k × (1 - p)**(n - k)`. Its mean is `n × p` and its variance `n × p × (1 - p)`.

The normal distribution is the symmetric bell curve described by a mean and a standard deviation (lesson 10). Sums and averages of many independent, similar contributions tend toward it, which is why sample means and measurement errors are often close to normal. About 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two and 99.7% within three.

A z-score `(x - mean) / sd` says how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean. Python's `statistics.NormalDist` gives probabilities directly through `cdf`, the probability of a value at or below x.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: With 20 requests that each fail 10% of the time, there is about a 12% chance of no failures and a 96% chance of at most four. For response sizes with mean 200 KB and standard deviation 20 KB, the three intervals reproduce the 68-95-99.7 rule, and about 0.6% of responses exceed 250 KB.
sections.example:
from math import comb
from statistics import NormalDist

n, p = 20, 0.1
pmf = [comb(n, k) * p**k * (1 - p)**(n - k) for k in range(n + 1)]
print(f'P(0 failures) = {pmf[0]:.4f}, P(at most 4) = {sum(pmf[:5]):.4f}, mean = {n * p}')

sizes = NormalDist(mu=200, sigma=20)
for k in (1, 2, 3):
    print(f'within {k} sd: {sizes.cdf(200 + 20 * k) - sizes.cdf(200 - 20 * k):.4f}')
print(f'above 250: {1 - sizes.cdf(250):.4f}')

# Expected output:
# P(0 failures) = 0.1216, P(at most 4) = 0.9568, mean = 2.0
# within 1 sd: 0.6827
# within 2 sd: 0.9545
# within 3 sd: 0.9973
# above 250: 0.0062

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: The binomial model needs independent trials with the same probability. Requests that fail together during an outage are not independent, so the real chance of many failures is far higher than the binomial predicts.

Many real measurements are skewed or heavy-tailed: latency, file sizes, incomes. A mean and standard deviation then describe them poorly, and the 68-95-99.7 rule understates extreme values. Plot the data and compare percentiles before assuming a normal shape.

exercise.prompt: A batch job retries each of 10 independent tasks that fail with probability 0.05. Find the probability that all 10 succeed and the probability that two or more fail. Then name a situation where this model would mislead.
exercise.solution:
P(all succeed) = 0.95**10 ≈ 0.5987.
P(exactly 1 fails) = 10 × 0.05 × 0.95**9 ≈ 0.3151.
P(2 or more) = 1 - 0.5987 - 0.3151 ≈ 0.0861.
It misleads when failures share a cause, such as a database outage that makes all tasks fail together.
checks: Uses the complement for 'two or more'.
Applies the binomial formula for exactly one failure.
Names dependence between failures as the model's weakness.

quiz.question: Values follow a normal distribution with mean 50 and standard deviation 5. Roughly what share lies between 40 and 60?
quiz.explanation: 40 and 60 are two standard deviations from the mean, and about 95% of a normal distribution lies within two.

lessons.title: 17. Interpret a confidence interval
lessons.takeaway: Across repeated samples, a 95% confidence-interval method captures the population mean about 95% of the time, under its assumptions.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A sample mean estimates a population mean and changes across samples. Under independent sampling with known population standard deviation sigma, the standard error of the mean is sigma/sqrt(n). For a normal population, a 95% interval is mean plus or minus about 1.96 standard errors.

The 95% statement describes the procedure: over repeated samples, about 95% of intervals cover the fixed population mean under the assumptions. It does not mean 95% of individual observations lie inside an interval for the mean. An interval also does not correct selection bias or an incorrect measurement process.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Suppose independent measurements come from a normal population with known sigma=10 ms. A sample of 100 has mean 50 ms. Standard error is 1 ms and the interval is approximately [48.04,51.96] ms. If sigma were merely estimated from a small sample, this known-sigma calculation would not be justified.
sections.example:
from math import sqrt
mean, sigma, n = 50, 10, 100
margin = 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n)
print(mean - margin, mean + margin)  # 48.04 51.96

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: Standard deviation describes the spread of observations. Standard error describes how much an estimator varies across samples. They answer different questions.

exercise.prompt: Under the same known-sigma normal model, increase n from 100 to 400 while holding sigma=10. What happens to the standard error and margin?
exercise.solution:
Standard error becomes 10/sqrt(400)=0.5.
Margin becomes 1.96*0.5=0.98.
Quadrupling n halves these quantities.
checks: Keep the assumptions explicit.
Do not say the observations became less variable.
hints: Standard error is sigma divided by the square root of n.
The margin is 1.96 standard errors.
pitfalls: Saying the observations became less variable.
Dividing by n instead of the square root of n.

quiz.question: A 95% interval for mean latency is [48,52] ms. Which claim follows?
options: The method targets the population mean under its assumptions
Every future sample mean will be inside it
quiz.explanation: This interval estimates a mean. It is neither a range for individual requests nor a guarantee about future samples.

practice.prompt: Same model, sigma = 10 ms, but only 25 measurements, with mean 50 ms. Supply the standard error, the margin and the 95% interval.
hints: The square root of 25 is 5.
practice.solution: Standard error = 10 / √25 = 2 ms. Margin = 1.96 × 2 = 3.92 ms. The interval is 50 ± 3.92, about [46.08, 53.92] ms, four times wider than with 400 measurements.
checks: Computes the standard error.
Computes the margin and the interval.

practice.prompt: How many measurements would make the 95% margin 0.5 ms with sigma = 10 ms?
hints: Square both sides after isolating √n.
practice.solution: Solve 1.96 × 10 / √n = 0.5: √n = 39.2, so n = 1,536.64. Round up to 1,537 measurements. Halving a margin needs four times as many observations, so precision gets expensive quickly.
checks: Rearranges the margin formula for n.
Rounds up.

practice.prompt: Use a 99% interval instead, with z ≈ 2.576, for the lesson's 100 measurements. What is the interval, and why is it wider?
hints: Only the multiplier changes.
practice.solution: Standard error is still 1 ms, so the margin is 2.576 ms and the interval is about [47.424, 52.576] ms. To cover the true mean in 99% of repeated samples instead of 95%, the procedure must use wider intervals.
checks: Uses the new z value.
Explains the wider interval through coverage.

practice.prompt: The team wants to promise that individual requests finish within the 95% interval for the mean latency, [48.04, 51.96] ms. Is that a valid promise?
hints: What does sigma = 10 ms say about individual requests?
practice.solution: No. The interval describes uncertainty about the mean, not where individual requests fall; with sigma = 10 ms, many requests are far outside it. For individual requests, use percentiles of the observed latencies, such as p95 or p99.
checks: Distinguishes the mean's interval from individual spread.
Proposes percentiles.

lessons.title: 18. Test a claim and read a p-value correctly
lessons.takeaway: A p-value measures how surprising the data would be if there were no effect; it is not the probability the effect is real, and it says nothing about its size.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A hypothesis test starts from a null hypothesis, usually "no difference", and a test statistic that measures how far the data are from it. The p-value is the probability, if the null hypothesis were true, of a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. A small p-value means the data would be unusual under the null.

Choose the significance level (often 0.05) before looking. If p is below it, reject the null; otherwise, say the data do not show a difference, not that there is none. With that rule, about 5% of tests of true null hypotheses still come out "significant": a false positive. Missing a real effect is a false negative, which small samples make likely.

A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and not the probability the result happened by chance. It also does not measure size: with enough data a trivial difference is significant. Report the estimated difference with a confidence interval (lesson 17) alongside the test.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: An A/B test shows 40 of 500 visitors converting with the old page and 58 of 500 with the new one. A two-proportion z-test gives z ≈ 1.92 and p ≈ 0.056: just above 0.05, so this test alone does not reject "no difference", though the estimate favours the new page. Running 20 independent tests on changes with no real effect gives a 64% chance that at least one looks significant.
sections.example:
from math import sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist

a_conv, a_n, b_conv, b_n = 40, 500, 58, 500
pooled = (a_conv + b_conv) / (a_n + b_n)
se = sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * (1 / a_n + 1 / b_n))
z = (b_conv / b_n - a_conv / a_n) / se
p_value = 2 * (1 - NormalDist().cdf(abs(z)))
print(f'difference = {b_conv / b_n - a_conv / a_n:.3f}, z = {z:.3f}, p = {p_value:.4f}')
print(f'P(at least one false positive in 20 tests) = {1 - 0.95**20:.4f}')

# Expected output:
# difference = 0.036, z = 1.915, p = 0.0556
# P(at least one false positive in 20 tests) = 0.6415

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: Decide the sample size, metric and stopping rule before the test. Checking repeatedly and stopping as soon as p < 0.05, or testing many metrics and reporting the best, inflates false positives; correct for multiple comparisons or pre-register one primary metric.

The z-test assumes independent observations and large enough counts. Visitors who return several times, or rates computed per session instead of per user, break independence. A significant result also depends on random assignment (lesson 23) to support a causal claim.

exercise.prompt: A colleague reports: "p = 0.03, so there is a 97% chance the new checkout increases revenue." Rewrite the conclusion correctly, and list what else you would ask for.
exercise.solution: Correct reading: if the new checkout made no difference, data at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time. It is not a 97% probability that the change works. Ask for the estimated effect size with a confidence interval, whether the metric, sample size and stopping rule were fixed in advance, how many other metrics or variants were tested, and whether assignment was random and observations independent.
checks: States the p-value as a probability of data given no effect.
Asks for effect size and an interval.
Asks about pre-registration, multiple comparisons and independence.
hints: A p-value assumes the null hypothesis is true and asks how surprising the data are.
Which numbers would tell you how large the effect is?
pitfalls: Reading p as the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
Reporting significance without an effect size.

quiz.question: A test gives p = 0.20. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The data do not provide strong evidence of an effect
There is a 20% chance the effect is real
quiz.explanation: A large p-value means the data are not unusual under the null hypothesis. It does not prove the null; small samples often miss real effects.

practice.prompt: Repeat the lesson's A/B test with twice the traffic and the same rates: 80 of 1,000 and 116 of 1,000 convert. Supply z and the two-sided p-value using the lesson's code.
hints: Change only the four counts in the example.

practice.prompt: Twenty independent tests of changes with no real effect gave a 64% chance of at least one false positive. With a Bonferroni correction, each test uses 0.05 / 20. What is the chance now?
hints: Compute the chance that all 20 tests stay non-significant first.

practice.prompt: For the lesson's z ≈ 1.915, what is the one-sided p-value for 'the new page is better', and when is a one-sided test legitimate?
hints: The two-sided p-value counts both tails.
practice.solution: One-sided p = 1 − Φ(1.915) ≈ 0.0278, half the two-sided value. It is legitimate only if the direction was declared before the data were seen and a result in the other direction would lead to the same decision as no difference. Switching to one-sided after seeing p = 0.056 is p-hacking.
checks: Halves the two-sided p-value.
Requires the direction to be declared in advance.

practice.prompt: With 10 million users per arm, the new page improves conversion by 0.01 percentage points, p = 0.001. Should you ship it?
hints: What does a large sample do to the p-value of a tiny effect?
practice.solution: Significance only says the difference is unlikely to be noise; with 10 million users even tiny effects are significant. Look at the effect size and its interval: 0.01 points may not cover the cost of building and maintaining the change. Decide on the practical value, not the p-value.
checks: Separates statistical significance from practical size.
Weighs effect against cost.

lessons.title: 19. Represent a record as a vector
lessons.takeaway: Each coordinate needs a fixed meaning and unit.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A real vector is an ordered list of numbers. For a document, `[word_count, link_count]` is a different representation from `[link_count, word_count]`. Equal lengths are necessary for addition, but matching coordinate meanings are necessary for a useful result.

Vector addition combines corresponding coordinates. Multiplying by a scalar multiplies every coordinate by the same number. The Euclidean length is sqrt(sum(x*x)). Using that length to compare heterogeneous features can make a large-unit feature dominate, so choose a representation before interpreting distance.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Weekly study totals [2,3] and [1,4] hours for Python and SQL add to [3,7]. The first vector has Euclidean length sqrt(13), but that length is not total study hours; its coordinate sum is 5.
sections.example:
from math import sqrt
a, b = [2,3], [1,4]
print([x+y for x,y in zip(a,b)])  # [3,7]
print(sqrt(sum(x*x for x in a)))  # about 3.606

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: Plain zip silently truncates mismatched lengths. Validate dimensions before using it for a vector operation.

exercise.prompt: For a=[3,4], calculate 2a and its Euclidean length. Explain why [3000,4] has a different length if only the first coordinate changes from metres to millimetres.
exercise.solution:
2a=[6,8], with length 10.
Changing one coordinate unit changes the numerical distance calculation. Convert to compatible units before interpreting a geometric length.
checks: Scale every coordinate.
Name the unit inconsistency.

options: No, coordinate meanings must also match
Only when their entries are positive
quiz.explanation: The operation exists numerically, but adding users to seconds has no useful interpretation without a model for those coordinates.

lessons.title: 20. Calculate a weighted score
lessons.takeaway: A dot product multiplies matching coordinates and adds the products.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: For vectors x and w of equal length, their dot product is sum(x_i*w_i). This can represent total cost, a weighted score or part of a geometric comparison. The meaning comes from the coordinate definitions and weights, not from the operation alone.

For nonzero vectors, dividing the dot product by both lengths gives cosine similarity. It measures direction rather than magnitude. A zero vector has no direction, so this normalization is undefined. A high similarity in your chosen representation does not prove that two documents mean the same thing.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: A basket contains three pens and two notebooks. Prices are 10 and 40 cents, so its dot product with the quantity vector is 3*10+2*40=110 cents.
sections.example:
quantities, prices = [3,2], [10,40]
print(sum(q*p for q,p in zip(quantities, prices)))  # 110

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: Weights can be negative and need not sum to one. A weighted average divides by the weight sum and normally states additional assumptions about those weights.

exercise.solution:
Dot product = 4+0-3 = 1.
The perpendicular unit vectors have dot product 0 and lengths 1, so cosine similarity is 0.
checks: Include the negative contribution.
Do not call zero similarity a proof of statistical independence.

lessons.title: 21. Multiply a matrix by a vector
lessons.takeaway: Each output is one row dotted with the input vector.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers. An m by n matrix maps an n-coordinate input vector to an m-coordinate output by taking one dot product per row. Write the dimensions before calculating; the number of columns must match the input length.

For matrix multiplication AB, each entry uses a row of A and a column of B. If A has shape m by n and B has shape n by p, the result has shape m by p. The inner dimensions must match. Multiplication order matters because the operations compose in that order.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Two baskets have quantities [3,2] and [1,4]. Multiplying their two-row quantity matrix by prices [10,40] gives basket costs [110,170]. Rows represent baskets and columns represent products.
sections.example:
baskets = [[3,2], [1,4]]
prices = [10,40]
print([sum(q*p for q,p in zip(row, prices)) for row in baskets])
# [110, 170]

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: A ragged nested list is not a rectangular matrix. Reject rows with inconsistent lengths instead of accepting partial dot products.

exercise.prompt: Multiply [[1,2,0],[0,1,3]] by [4,5,6]. State the matrix shape and result shape.
exercise.solution:
The matrix is 2 by 3.
Row results are 1*4+2*5+0*6=14 and 0*4+1*5+3*6=23.
The result [14,23] has two coordinates.
checks: Compute each row separately.
An input with two coordinates must be rejected.

quiz.question: A is 2 by 3 and B is 3 by 4. What is the shape of AB?
quiz.explanation: The shared inner dimension is three. Two rows of A and four columns of B produce a 2 by 4 result.

lessons.title: 22. Read association without claiming a cause
lessons.takeaway: Correlation summarizes a pattern; it does not identify why the pattern occurs.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Pearson correlation compares paired deviations from each variable mean after scaling by their spread. It lies between -1 and 1 when defined. A value near 1 describes a strong positive linear pattern, while a value near 0 means little linear association, not necessarily no relationship.

Pairs must refer to the same units of observation. Shuffling only one column destroys the pairings. A third variable can influence both observed variables. Reverse causation and selection can also explain an association. A causal claim needs a design and assumptions that address these alternatives.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: For x=[1,2,3] and y=[2,4,6], y is exactly 2x, so Pearson correlation is 1. Changing y to [-2,-4,-6] makes it -1. Neither calculation tells us whether changing x would change y in a real system.
sections.example:
from statistics import correlation
print(correlation([1,2,3], [2,4,6]))  # 1.0

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: Correlation with a constant variable is undefined because that variable has zero spread. Zero correlation can also hide a curved relationship, such as y=x*x on symmetric x values.

exercise.prompt: Teams with more incidents also write more incident reports. Give a plausible direction of causation and explain why deleting reports is not a supported remedy.
exercise.solution: Incidents can cause teams to write reports. Reports may therefore track incidents without causing them. Removing reports could hide incidents rather than prevent them.
checks: Identify reverse causation.
Do not infer intervention effects from an observed correlation.
hints: Which comes first in time, the incident or its report?
What would deleting reports change: the incidents, or what you can see of them?
pitfalls: Inferring that changing one variable changes the other from a correlation.

quiz.question: Pearson correlation is zero. Which conclusion is justified?
options: There is no linear association captured by this statistic
Changing either variable cannot affect the other
quiz.explanation: A zero value rules out this measured linear pattern, not nonlinear relationships or causal effects.

references.section: mean, median, pvariance, variance and correlation
references.scope: Python 3.14 APIs; descriptions distinguish population summaries from sample estimates.

practice.prompt: Compute the Pearson correlation for x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and y = [2, 4, 5, 4, 5] with `statistics.correlation`, and describe the pattern.
hints: Use `statistics.correlation(x, y)`.
practice.solution: The correlation is about 0.775: a fairly strong positive linear association, though y does not rise at every step. With only five points, one changed value would move it a lot, so report the data alongside the number.
checks: Computes the coefficient.
Comments on the small sample.

practice.prompt: Now y = x² for x = [−2, −1, 0, 1, 2]. What is the correlation, and what does it miss?
hints: Positive and negative x values give the same y.
practice.solution: The correlation is 0. y is completely determined by x, but the relationship is a U shape, and Pearson correlation measures only straight-line association. Plot the data before concluding there is no relationship.
checks: Computes the coefficient.
Explains that the relationship is not linear.

practice.prompt: Across cities, ice-cream sales and swimming accidents are correlated. Name the likely third variable and describe how you would check it with the data you have.
hints: What drives both variables up in summer?
practice.solution: Hot weather increases both ice-cream sales and swimming, and so accidents. Compare the association within groups of similar temperature, or include temperature in a regression. If the association largely disappears within those groups, temperature explains it. This removes only the confounders you measure.
checks: Names the confounder.
Proposes stratifying or adjusting.
Notes the limit to measured confounders.

practice.prompt: Teams that attended a reliability course have fewer incidents. A manager wants to make the course mandatory to cut incidents. Does the data support that?
hints: Who decided which teams attended?
practice.solution: Not on its own. Teams that chose to attend may already care more about reliability, or have simpler systems: selection and confounding. To estimate the course's effect, randomise which teams attend first, or compare incident trends before and after attendance against similar teams that have not yet attended.
checks: Names selection or confounding.
Proposes a randomised or comparative design.

lessons.title: 23. Plan a comparison that can answer a causal question
lessons.takeaway: Random assignment helps separate a treatment from pre-existing group differences.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: An observational comparison records what already happened. An experiment assigns a treatment. If faster machines all receive a new algorithm, observed speed can reflect hardware rather than the algorithm. Random assignment reduces systematic treatment-group differences in expectation; it does not guarantee perfectly balanced small groups.

Choose the assignment unit, outcome and analysis before seeing the result. Repeated requests on the same machine can share conditions, so treating them as independent machines overstates the available information. Keep hardware and measurement rules comparable and report missing results.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: A fictional benchmark compares old and new versions on matched inputs. Alternate their run order after a random start, include warm-up rules and measure the same output checks. If the new version produces wrong answers, its speed alone does not satisfy the task.
sections.example:
from random import Random
units = list(range(8))
Random(7).shuffle(units)
a, b = units[:4], units[4:]
print(len(a), len(b), set(a).isdisjoint(b))  # 4 4 True

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: A seed gives a reproducible assignment. It does not eliminate interference between units, changes during the experiment or selective reporting.

exercise.prompt: A team deploys a faster cache only to its newest servers. Propose a comparison that reduces the hardware confound and name one remaining limitation.
exercise.solution: Randomly assign cache versions within groups of similar hardware, with the same workload and correctness checks. Shared traffic or cache warm-up can still affect results and must be measured or controlled.
checks: Change assignment, not just the chart.
Retain a concrete remaining threat to interpretation.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of random assignment?
options: Guarantee identical groups in every experiment
Remove the need for a control group
Reduce systematic pre-existing differences between treatment groups
quiz.explanation: Random assignment balances differences in expectation. Chance imbalance and design failures remain possible.

lessons.title: 24. Choose a scale before measuring distance
lessons.takeaway: A coordinate unit can change a distance-based comparison.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: If one coordinate records bytes and another records seconds, their numerical magnitudes can differ greatly. Euclidean distance adds squared coordinate differences, so the large-scale feature may dominate. Dividing each feature by a stated reference scale changes what counts as a large difference.

One common transformation subtracts a training mean and divides by a training standard deviation. It centres that feature at zero and expresses differences in standard-deviation units. Fit these values only on the training data before applying them to held-out data. A constant feature has zero standard deviation and needs an explicit policy rather than division by zero.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: For training values [2,4,6], use mean 4 and population standard deviation sqrt(8/3) for this illustrative transformation. The centre value becomes zero. A future value 8 becomes about 2.449 using the same fixed training parameters.
sections.example:
from statistics import mean, pstdev
train = [2,4,6]
centre, scale = mean(train), pstdev(train)
print((8-centre)/scale)  # about 2.449

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: Scaling does not establish that every feature deserves equal influence. A chosen scale and a chosen weight each encode a modeling decision; inspect whether the decision changes under reasonable alternatives.

exercise.prompt: Training mean is 10 and standard deviation is 2. Transform 14. Should you recompute the mean using the held-out value before transforming it? Explain.
exercise.solution:
The transformed value is (14-10)/2=2.
Keep the fitted training parameters. Recomputing them from held-out data changes the evaluation procedure and leaks information from the held-out set.
checks: Subtract before dividing.
Preserve the fitted parameters for later data.

quiz.question: A feature has the same value in every training row. What happens to standard-deviation scaling?
options: It needs a policy because the denominator is zero
quiz.explanation: A constant feature has no observed variation. Dropping it or mapping it by an explicit convention avoids undefined division.

lessons.title: 25. Combine calculation with an honest conclusion
lessons.takeaway: State the decision, the numerical result and what the comparison cannot establish.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A useful report separates observed results from assumptions and proposed actions. First check units, valid inputs and denominators. Then calculate the relevant summaries. Finally connect the result to the actual decision, such as whether a proposed scoring rule meets a stated budget.

A weighted score is a model choice. Test whether a reasonable change in weights changes the ranking. If it does, the decision depends on the preference encoded by those weights. Confidence in arithmetic does not remove that preference or uncertainty in the data.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Candidate A has normalized benefit scores [0.9,0.4] and B has [0.6,0.8]. Weights [0.8,0.2] give A=0.80 and B=0.64. Equal weights give A=0.65 and B=0.70. The preferred candidate changes, so report that dependence instead of declaring an unconditional winner.
sections.example:
candidates = [[0.9,0.4], [0.6,0.8]]
for weights in ([0.8,0.2], [0.5,0.5]):
    print([round(sum(x*w for x,w in zip(row,weights)),2) for row in candidates])
# [0.8, 0.64]
# [0.65, 0.7]

sections.title: Check the assumption
paragraphs: A synthetic exercise can verify calculations and reasoning. It cannot establish how a real deployment will perform or replace a properly designed evaluation.

exercise.prompt: Complete the advanced project. Report both score rankings, check one invalid shape and explain why a before/after latency reduction alone does not prove the scoring change caused it.
exercise.solution: The reference prints [0.8,0.64] then [0.65,0.7]. A vector of the wrong length raises ValueError. Traffic, hardware or timing changes could explain before/after latency, so a controlled comparison is needed for a causal claim.
checks: Report the rank reversal.
Show the dimension failure.
Name a plausible confound rather than claiming proof.

quiz.question: Two reasonable weight sets choose different winners. What should the report say?
options: Report the dependence and ask which trade-off matches the decision
Average the winners into a causal claim
quiz.explanation: The weights express a preference. Reporting sensitivity lets the decision-maker judge that preference.
